The central bank’s chief economist urged the government on 20 November to stop changing the bank’s mandate.
554.b: High fuel prices raise transport and agricultural costs.
src: Bloomberg: NZ Central Bank’s Chief Economist Urges Government to Stop Messing With Mandate (20 Nov)

152.s: A stable democracy with a new government focused on crime.
i: Organised crime
Transnational gangs have driven a rise in violent crime.
Copper and lithium policy
Mining rules and royalties matter greatly to investors.
Fuel price strikes
Truckers began an indefinite strike over fuel prices on 11 November, and northern regions have joined.
152.b: Copper and lithium producers benefit from demand, but crime and mining-policy shifts affect costs.
src: Rio Times: Latin American Pulse (12 Nov)

068.s: A deep economic crisis under a new government pushing painful reforms.
i: Economic crisis
Fuel and dollar shortages, high inflation and low reserves strain the economy.
Subsidy cuts and reform
The government that took office in November 2025 is pushing reforms, including cuts to fuel subsidies.
Organised crime and politics
Authorities arrested a former judge on suspicion of drug trafficking as a new legislative term began.
068.b: Fuel and dollar shortages, blockades and policy shifts make operations and payments unpredictable.
src: Al Jazeera: Latin America news (12 Nov)

012.s: A gas supplier with unsettled borders.
i: Sahel border insecurity
Instability in Mali and Niger threatens Algeria’s long southern border.
Gas export leverage
Higher demand for its gas raises Algeria’s importance to Europe.
Fiscal resilience
The World Bank highlighted Algeria’s reliance on hydrocarbon revenues and the need for fiscal buffers in a 19 November assessment.
012.b: Europe’s need for non-Russian gas raises Algeria’s value as a supplier, but state control limits foreign investment.
src: World Bank: Algeria: Using Hydrocarbon Revenues and Fiscal Resilience (19 Nov)

504.s: Stable, with youth discontent and Western Sahara diplomacy in focus.
i: Youth protests
Gen Z-led protests over health and education spending erupted in 2025.
Western Sahara
A 2025 UN Security Council resolution backed Morocco’s autonomy plan, but the dispute is not settled.
Leadership and defence
Morocco now has its first woman prime minister, appointed on the palace’s terms, and launched a plan to build up its domestic defence industry.
504.b: A stable base for manufacturing and exports, though youth protests signal social pressure.
src: LSE blogs: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister: Progress on the Palace’s Terms (19 Nov)
Global Arab Network: Morocco Launches Ambitious Plan to Bolster Domestic Defense Industry (19 Nov)

i: Authoritarian consolidation
Critics, journalists and opposition figures face arrest and prosecution.
Debt and shortages
Weak finances have led to periodic shortages of basic goods.
Economy and external finance
Japan lent Tunisia ¥9.6 billion to complete the Sfax desalination plant, and olive oil exports hit a record 5.2 billion dinars.
788.b: Repression and shortages raise operational and reputational risk.
src: Smart Water Magazine: Japan lends Tunisia ¥9.6bn to finish remaining works at Sfax desalination plant (20 Nov)
The Arab Weekly: Tunisia’s olive oil export revenues hit record 5.2 billion dinars (19 Nov)

288.s: A stable democracy rebuilding after a debt crisis.
i: Illegal gold mining
Galamsey mining pollutes rivers and fuels local conflict.
Debt restructuring
Recovery depends on fiscal discipline after the 2022 default.
Spending controversy
A $60 million presidential jet purchase has sparked controversy as Ghana plans curbs on raw cashew exports and seeks Chinese support for its economic programme.
288.b: Gold and cocoa exporters face illegal mining, debt pressure and northern security risks.
src: France 24: Ghana's $60 million presidential jet purchase sparks controversy (20 Nov)
Forbes Africa: Ghana’s 262,000-Ton Cashew Industry Faces Export Curbs Under Government’s New Plan (20 Nov)

508.s: An insurgency in the north and a fragile political settlement.
i: Cabo Delgado insurgency
Islamic State-linked fighters still attack villages and roads in the north.
Post-election tensions
The trial of opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane is testing judicial independence, while the government has pledged over three billion meticais to repair damage from post-election unrest.
Post-election tensions
Deadly unrest followed the disputed 2024 election.
508.b: Gas projects in the north depend on security improving in Cabo Delgado.
src: Mail & Guardian: Mozambique's Mondlane trial puts judicial independence and rule of law under scrutiny (20 Nov)
Club of Mozambique: Mozambique: Chapo announces over three billion meticais for reconstruction of public infra (20 Nov)

834.s: Political repression after a violent election.
i: Post-election crackdown
Security forces killed protesters after the disputed October 2025 election.
Political repression
Opposition leaders face arrest and restrictions.
Constitutional reform
President Hassan pledged a new constitution as early as 2028, a year after the contested 2025 election.
834.b: Political repression and unrest weigh on investor confidence.
src: Bloomberg: Tanzania’s Hassan Pledges New Constitution as Early as 2028 (20 Nov)

048.s: Host of the US Fifth Fleet, now directly targeted by Iran.
048.b: Iranian strikes put US-linked facilities, Gulf shipping and the financial sector at risk.
i: Iranian attacks
An Iranian strike on 21 November caused a fire at a civilian industrial facility; the IRGC says it targeted US Patriot air-defence sites, and neighbouring states condemned the attack.
US Fifth Fleet host
As home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, Bahrain sits on Iran’s stated target list.
Hormuz exposure
Its oil and aluminium exports depend on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
src: ABC News: IRGC says Bahrain attacks targeted US Patriot sites (22 Nov)
Gulf News: Bahrain intercepts Iranian attacks as Tehran prepares tankers to breach blockade (22 Nov)
CBS News: Bahrain and Kuwait intercept Iranian weapons (19 Nov)

262.s: A Bab el-Mandeb gateway hosting foreign bases, squeezed by wars on both shores.
262.b: The main port for Ethiopian trade and a base for US, French and Chinese forces.
i: Two-coast conflict
The Houthis now hold the opposite shore of the Bab el-Mandeb, while fighting in Ethiopia’s Afar region threatens the Addis Ababa–Djibouti corridor.
Ethiopia–Eritrea tensions
G7 ministers warned on 10 November of regional escalation; a war could disrupt the corridor that carries over 90% of Ethiopia’s trade.
Foreign military presence
US, French, Chinese and other bases make Djibouti strategically valuable but exposed.
src: Addis Standard via allAfrica: G7 warns of regional escalation (11 Nov)
Modern Diplomacy: Both shores of the Bab el-Mandeb are now at war

232.s: On the brink of war with Ethiopia over sea access and the port of Assab.
232.b: Red Sea coastline and the port of Assab make any conflict a shipping risk.
i: Border clashes with Ethiopia
Eritrean and Ethiopian forces exchanged fire near Badme in November, raising fears of a wider war.
Assab and the Red Sea
Ethiopia’s demand for sea access, with references to Assab, is the core of the dispute, near the Bab el-Mandeb.
Isolation
Eritrea has no diplomatic ties with Ethiopia; US sanctions imposed in 2021 were lifted in September 2026.
src: Rio Times: Africa Intelligence Brief (21 Nov)
DW via allAfrica: Ethiopia–Eritrea border clashes raise fears of war (17 Nov)
Brookings: Pulling Eritrea and Ethiopia back from the brink (12 Nov)
Small Wars Journal: A second Red Sea front (3 Nov)

702.s: A stable hub now on the front line of US chip export controls.
702.b: Data centres, chip trading and shipping finance face tighter US scrutiny.
i: US chip export rules
New US rules from 16 November require licences for advanced chips going to data centres in Singapore and four other countries that could serve Chinese customers.
Megaspeed scrutiny
Singapore data-centre firm Megaspeed is under scrutiny over possible diversion of Nvidia chips to China; it says it complies with all laws.
Shipping hub
Busy Malacca and Singapore Strait traffic keeps the port central to Asian trade as Middle East routes are disrupted.
src: Al Jazeera: US moves to block China’s remote access to AI chips (17 Nov)
The Edge Malaysia: US tightens chip curbs; Megaspeed statement (17 Nov)

116.s: A tense, unresolved border dispute with Thailand a year after the peace accord.
116.b: Border closures and displacement disrupt cross-border trade and labour flows.
i: Thai border dispute
ASEAN observers reported Thai troops moving a post forward and digging trenches in early November; Cambodia protested Thai road building on 13 November.
Displacement
Nearly 8,000 residents of one border checkpoint area still cannot return home, according to Cambodia’s defence ministry.
Diplomacy
Prime Minister Hun Manet said on 19 November that Trump had pledged continued US support for border peace.
src: Asia News Network: ASEAN observers report forward movement of Thai post (6 Nov)
Cambodianess: Cambodia protests Thai road construction (13 Nov)
Phnom Penh Post: Manet shares Trump’s pledge (19 Nov)

591.s: Canal operations have recovered, but the fight over its ports is now in the courts.
591.b: Canal capacity and port control matter for global shipping and US–China rivalry.
i: Ports dispute
The state auditor filed a criminal complaint on 17 November against CK Hutchison’s Panama Ports Company, which lost control of the canal’s two main ports in February.
Canal capacity
The canal restored 34 daily transits and full draft on 11 November as water levels recovered from drought.
US–China competition
Who controls infrastructure at both ends of the canal remains a point of US–China friction.
src: Rio Times: Panama auditor files complaint over ports (17 Nov)
gCaptain: Panama Canal raises daily transit capacity (11 Nov)

items: About 25 tankers hit around Hormuz in a week; Iran plans to run tankers through the US blockade.
Iranian strike sets fire to an industrial site in Bahrain.
Somalia expels the UAE ambassador, alleging an ‘open invasion’.
Russian missiles hit Polish territory; Moscow denies.
Updates across 23 countries, chokepoints and events.
The ICJ rules that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya; Myanmar and China reject the ruling.
Somalia expels the UAE ambassador, accusing Abu Dhabi of violating its sovereignty.
Gap review: 50 country briefs refreshed with dated sources; Bahrain, Djibouti, Eritrea, Singapore, Cambodia and Panama added; Suez, Malacca, Panama and Danish Straits updated.
Trump, Xi and Putin meet in Shenzhen: a “peace declaration” on nuclear risk and energy supplies that does not mention Iran or Ukraine.
Iran steps up attacks on Hormuz shipping; at least two seafarers are missing after strikes this week.
A Houthi strike damages the PIF tower in Riyadh as coalition jets hit Sanaa.
Maritime risk page updated: new outlooks for Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and the Black Sea, the Kerch Strait, and new incidents.
Denmark’s parliament approves a security deal with Greenland and the US.
Ukraine hits the Kerch Bridge railway section, halting trains, two days after a road span collapsed into the strait.
Russian drones strike Odesa’s historic centre, killing four; the city declares a day of mourning.
Houthi forces push east along the Gulf of Aden coast towards Aden.
US strikes Qeshm Island after IRGC attacks; Iran targets Bahrain and Kuwait.
An ADNOC vessel is attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi-led coalition launches a major air campaign against the Houthis.
New: live headlines for every country and chokepoint, refreshed automatically every three hours.
Quad leaders meet in Manila for the first time since 2024: joint maritime patrols, critical minerals deals and a warning on economic coercion that does not name China.
Thailand and the US reach the substance of a reciprocal trade deal.
Iran and Oman hold talks in Muscat on shipping and maritime security; no deal announced.
A tanker is attacked off Oman overnight.
Houthi forces reportedly push towards Aden after taking the Bab el-Mandeb coast.
Estonia says it will close its road crossings with Russia on 1 December after a GRU-linked sabotage plot.
The Houthis take control of the Bab el-Mandeb coastline after government forces withdraw.
Iran says three tankers hit mines and a supertanker sank; drones launched at a US site in Bahrain.
Ukrainian drones halt Rosneft’s Ryazan refinery.
Bab el-Mandeb, Hormuz and Suez chokepoints updated; US–Russia–China summit confirmed for 19 November.
Two more tankers hit mines in Hormuz; Trump weighs a pause on strikes and will raise Iran with Putin and Xi next week.
Russian barrage kills at least six in Kyiv; Zaporizhzhia strike injures 50.
Qatar and Türkiye sign a mutual defence pact.
Iran sets seven conditions for talks and claims a strike on an Omani island; Trump says the US does not need a deal.
Second full review: about 40 more countries updated, including Indonesia (vice president resigns), Bangladesh, Peru, Chile, Jordan, Iraq, Kenya and Germany.
Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb chokepoints updated.

New: economic snapshot for 93 countries from the IMF World Economic Outlook (October 2026), covering GDP growth, inflation, government debt and the current account, on the site and in downloadable briefs.
New: first company spotlight, on SeaLead and US sanctions on the Shamkhani shipping network, plus a redesigned downloadable brief with the economic snapshot at the bottom.
New: Megaspeed company spotlight, four risk themes, a compare tool, a risk-over-time chart, US sanctions exposure for every country, and a briefings archive of dated snapshots.
Abu Dhabi talks ended with a prisoner-swap deal in principle but no ceasefire.
Washington weighing Iran’s latest proposal; Qatar warns of a frozen conflict.
Faultline moved to new hosting; the contact form now opens your email app.
Full review of all 100 countries: about 30 updated with new developments and sources, including Israel, Sudan, DR Congo, Venezuela and Colombia.
New: shipping chokepoints layer on the globe, covering Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, Suez, the Bosporus, the Taiwan Strait, Malacca, Panama and the Danish Straits.
Trump paused new strikes after Gulf appeals but kept the blockade; Iran tabled a new proposal via Qatar.
Abu Dhabi talks opened, the first trilateral round since February.
White House holding off fresh strikes on Iran.
US tightened its blockade, disabling a cargo ship and launching a task force against Iran’s land supply routes.
US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi confirmed for 10–11 November.
New on the site: linked sources, Coming up, business impact, region view, country links and downloadable briefs.
Coverage expanded from 65 to 100 countries.
New US strikes on Qeshm Island; tankers hit mines near Hormuz.
Heavy Russian strikes on the power grid; peace talks expected.
US sanctions on Indian firms linked to Iranian tankers.
Lowered from Elevated to Guarded after the student-led list won a majority.
Democrats won both chambers of Congress.
Reported Israeli plans if Hezbollah joins a renewed Iran war.
US strike on Qeshm Island; Hormuz effectively closed.
No clear majority after the 27 October election.
Lula won the presidential runoff; his opponent has not conceded.

chokepoints.s: Closed to normal traffic. Oil still moves, mostly on ships running dark, at roughly half its pre-war volume.
i: Traffic far below normal
UKMTO counted 263 transits in the week to 18 November, about 65% below pre-war levels.
Mines and attacks
About 25 tankers have been hit since 14 November, two more on 22 November, and war-risk insurance is up to 3.5–7.5% of hull value.
Escalating attacks
Attacks rose in October and continued at that pace in November; the US struck Qeshm Island on 17–18 November and at least two seafarers are missing after this week’s strikes.
src: Al Jazeera: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf? (22 Nov)
GlobalSecurity: Iran War Day 267 update (21 Nov)
Bloomberg via News Tribune: Iran intensifies Hormuz tanker attacks (20 Nov)
The Boston Report: Middle East tanker flow tracker (18 Nov)

chokepoints.s: The Houthis hold almost all of Yemen’s shore on the strait and are pushing towards Aden.
i: Houthi control of the coast
Government-aligned forces withdrew on 15 November; Houthi forces have since moved east along the Gulf of Aden coast.
Ships contacting the Houthis
Some ships now email the Houthis’ coordination centre before transiting, a sign of the group’s growing leverage over the strait.
Depressed traffic
PortWatch counted about 26 transits a day in mid-November, roughly a third below the same week of 2025, as many shippers still sail around Africa.
src: Red Sea Futures: The Houthis menace Aden (19 Nov)
Long War Journal: Houthis retake Bab al Mandeb and move toward Aden (16 Nov)
Juan Cole: The march of the Houthis (19 Nov)

chokepoints.s: Europe’s shortest sea link to Asia, with traffic still depressed by Red Sea insecurity.
i: Diverted traffic
Suez transits were about 37% below 2023 levels in mid-November, and Houthi control of the Bab el-Mandeb coast makes a recovery less likely.
Egypt’s lost revenue
Lower canal income adds to Egypt’s debt and currency pressure.
Gulf war spillover
The Iran war raises insurance costs for all Middle East routes.
src: IMF PortWatch: Daily chokepoint transits (via Faultline maritime data)
Long War Journal: Houthis retake Bab al Mandeb (16 Nov)

chokepoints.s: The main sea route for Ukrainian and Russian Black Sea exports, now with the Kerch Strait disrupted as well.
i: Kerch Strait disrupted
Ukraine collapsed a 227-metre span of the Kerch Bridge on 17 November; experts expect the wreckage to disrupt Russian shipping through the strait for a long time.
Strikes on ports and ships
Russian drones struck Odesa’s historic centre on 18 November, and war-risk premiums for some Ukrainian ports rose to as much as 1% in early November.
Russian shadow fleet
Sanctioned Russian tankers transit the straits, adding spill and enforcement risk.
src: Interfax-Ukraine: Kerch Bridge strike to disrupt Russian shipping (17 Nov)
Interfax-Ukraine: Russian strikes on Odesa kill 4, injure 9 (18 Nov)
India Seatrade News: War-risk premiums jump in Black Sea (1 Nov)

chokepoints.s: A main artery for Asian trade and chip supply chains, under steady Chinese military pressure.
i: PLA coercion
Chinese ships and aircraft operate around Taiwan daily; Taiwan’s coast guard drove four Chinese ships from Kinmen waters on 10 November.
Blockade risk
A quarantine or blockade would disrupt shipping and semiconductor exports worldwide.
Insurance and rerouting
Any crisis would quickly raise war-risk premiums for Asian routes.
src: Pacific Winds: Indo-Pacific security digest (12 Nov)
IMF PortWatch: Daily chokepoint transits (via Faultline maritime data)

chokepoints.s: The busiest shipping lane between the Indian Ocean and East Asia.
i: Normal but busy
Traffic was close to normal in mid-November, at about 230 transits a day according to PortWatch, as the strait absorbs Asian trade diverted from troubled Middle East routes.
Piracy and armed robbery
Low-level robbery of ships continues in the Singapore Strait.
Chip export rules
New US licence requirements from 16 November for advanced-chip shipments to data centres in Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand put the strait’s tech hubs under closer scrutiny.
src: IMF PortWatch: Daily chokepoint transits (via Faultline maritime data)
Al Jazeera: US moves to block China’s remote access to AI chips (17 Nov)

chokepoints.s: The key link between the Atlantic and Pacific, at the centre of US–China competition over ports.
i: Capacity restored
The canal raised daily transit slots to 34 and restored full draft at the Neopanamax locks on 11 November as water levels improved; transits rose 4.1% in the year to September.
Ports dispute
Panama’s state auditor filed a criminal complaint on 17 November against CK Hutchison’s Panama Ports Company, which ran the ports at both ends of the canal until the state took them over in February.
Regional politics
The canal itself operates normally.
src: gCaptain: Panama Canal raises daily transit capacity (11 Nov)
Rio Times: Panama auditor files complaint over ports (17 Nov)
Seatrade Maritime: Panama Canal sees 4% growth in FY2026

chokepoints.s: The Baltic Sea’s gateway to the North Sea, used by Russia’s shadow fleet.
i: Shadow fleet transits
Sanctioned and shadow-fleet tankers are tracked transiting from Russia’s Baltic ports, and the EU’s 16 November sanctions targeted the Saint Petersburg oil terminal.
Undersea infrastructure
Cables and pipelines in the Baltic have been damaged in suspected sabotage.
Baltic hybrid threats
Estonia will close its road border with Russia on 1 December after a GRU-linked sabotage plot, part of a wave of sabotage across the region.
